title: Does AI Help Junior or Senior Developers More?

scenes.purpose: Set up the two developers the question is about.

visual.description: Dark field; two words build left and right, 'veteran' then 'newcomer', as the narration names them.
onScreenText: A veteran and a newcomer

scenes.direction: Cold open; line types on with the narration.
scenes.narration: Picture a pair of developers switching on the same AI coding assistant on the same morning: a veteran, and a newcomer just starting out.

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers.

visual.description: The question types on in large type; 'more' held in accent colour.
onScreenText: Which of them gets more out of it?

scenes.direction: Type on; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: Which of them gets more out of it?

scenes.purpose: Name the popular answer and the plan: test it against trials.

visual.description: Title line; 'the veteran' lands first, then the rest builds.
onScreenText: The confident answer: the veteran

scenes.direction: Line lands on 'the veteran'.
scenes.narration: The confident answer online is the veteran, so let's put that answer next to the trials that actually measured it.

scenes.purpose: The belief in its source's own words.

visual.description: Quote card with the quoted words only; 'the best engineers' turns accent as spoken.
onScreenText: "the AI agents are going to help the best engineers more than the mediocre engineer"

citations.label: The Pragmatic Engineer, episode on AI at Shopify

scenes.direction: Camera pushes in slowly through the quote.
scenes.narration: On The Pragmatic Engineer, in an episode about AI at Shopify, it was offered as a maybe: "the AI agents are going to help the best engineers more than the mediocre engineer".

scenes.purpose: A second voice for the same belief.

visual.description: Quote card with the quoted words only; 'run circles' punches in.
onScreenText: "run circles around somebody who's never written a code line of code in their life"

citations.label: Simon Willison on The Pragmatic Engineer

scenes.direction: Camera punches on 'run circles'.
scenes.narration: On the same show, Simon Willison said that with these tools he will "run circles around somebody who's never written a code line of code in their life".

scenes.purpose: Narrow the belief to what the trials can test.

visual.description: The testable question types on.
onScreenText: Did the best engineers gain more than the rest?

scenes.direction: Type on as the narration reaches the question; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: Willison's yardstick is someone who has never coded, and the trials that follow compared developers with each other, so what they can test is the first claim: when researchers split their results by experience, did the best engineers gain more than the rest?

scenes.purpose: First evidence: in the Copilot field experiments the gains leaned to short-tenure developers, with the noise stated.

visual.description: Two stat tiles side by side: short-tenure '27% to 39%' left, long-tenure '8% to 13%' right; the second tile arrives as the narration reaches it, then a small 'not statistically significant' line fades in under both on s08.

chart.title: Output gain with Copilot, by tenure
chart.note: Ranges across three output measures; estimates noisy and not statistically significant.

onScreenText: Noisy, not statistically significant

citations.label: Cui et al., Copilot field experiments

scenes.direction: Tiles build per sentence; caveat line on 'not statistically significant'.
scenes.narration: In field experiments that gave developers the coding assistant Copilot, short-tenure developers raised their output by 27 to 39 percent, while long-tenure developers gained 8 to 13 percent. Those estimates are noisy and not statistically significant, but the pattern was the same on all three of the studies' main output measures.

scenes.purpose: Show the authors' own caveat and why the direction holds.

visual.description: The cited paragraph from the paper; the phrase about equal usage after adoption highlights as the narration reaches it.

excerpt.highlight: no difference in usage conditional on adoption

citations.label: Cui et al., Copilot field experiments

scenes.direction: Slow scroll to the highlight; hold.
scenes.narration: The authors note that longer-tenure developers abandoning the tool after a trial may shrink their estimate, yet junior developers, who used it as much as seniors once they had adopted it, still gained more than senior ones.

scenes.purpose: Two more trials point the same way.

visual.description: List builds one line per sentence: first the separate experiment's finding, then the Copilot trial's.
onScreenText: Fewer years of experience: faster, quality unaffected
Less experienced programmers benefited more

citations.label: Shan et al., generative AI experiment

scenes.direction: Line two on 'less experienced programmers'.
scenes.narration: A separate experiment found the same direction: developers with fewer years of experience got the speed benefit from generative AI, while the quality of their code was unaffected. Another Copilot trial found that less experienced programmers benefited more, and its authors called that promising for people moving into software development, if the result holds up in further studies.

scenes.purpose: A trial across experience levels found gains for every group, not tied to experience.

visual.description: List builds one line per sentence: every group improved; professionals gained more, on harder tasks.
onScreenText: Every group got further with AI
Professionals gained more, on the most complex tasks

citations.label: Code-ownership experiment, BSc students to professionals

scenes.direction: Line two on 'Professionals gained more'.
scenes.narration: An experiment that ran from bachelor's students to professional developers found that every group got significantly further through its task with AI support, and its authors say the differences between groups were not related to experience. Professionals gained more there than bachelor's students, but each group had tasks suited to its level, and the professionals' were among the most complex.

scenes.purpose: Introduce METR's deeply experienced developers by how well they knew their repositories.

visual.description: Two stat tiles: '5 years' and '1,500 commits', each landing as spoken.

chart.title: Average experience in their own repositories

scenes.direction: Tiles punch in on '5 years' and '1,500 commits'.
scenes.narration: Then there is a trial of developers who knew their projects deeply: 5 years and 1,500 commits on average in the repositories they worked on.

scenes.purpose: Show that the experts were slower, and slowed more on familiar work, in the paper's words.

visual.description: The cited METR passage; 'moderate evidence' and 'high prior task exposure' highlight as the narration says them.

excerpt.highlight: less helpful when working on familiar ones

scenes.direction: Scroll to the highlight on 'less helpful on familiar ones'.
scenes.narration: With AI allowed, these developers were slower, not faster, and its researchers report moderate evidence that they were slowed down more on issues where they had high prior exposure to the task; the developers said AI was particularly helpful on unfamiliar issues and less helpful on familiar ones.

scenes.purpose: A maintainer's own words on why AI did not help.

visual.description: Quote card with the quoted words only.
onScreenText: "if I am the dedicated maintainer of a very specialized part of the codebase, there is no way agent mode can do better than me."

scenes.direction: Hold 0.5 s after the last word.
scenes.narration: As one developer put it: "if I am the dedicated maintainer of a very specialized part of the codebase, there is no way agent mode can do better than me."

scenes.purpose: The one trial that leaned toward seniors, with its non-significance and the authors' reading.

visual.description: List builds one line per sentence: the lean toward seniors with 'not statistically significant', then the authors' explanation.
onScreenText: Seniors faster with AI, not statistically significant
AI may not yet close a skill gap on complex tasks

scenes.direction: Line one on 'more senior engineers'; line two on 'skill gap'.
scenes.narration: One trial leaned the other way: on a complex task, more senior engineers were, if anything, faster with AI than less senior ones, though that difference was not statistically significant. Its authors suggest AI may not yet be able to close a skill gap on a task that complex.

scenes.purpose: Turn to the second half of the belief: tool skill.

visual.description: Question types on; 'skill' in accent.
onScreenText: Is using these tools well a skill of its own?

scenes.direction: Hard cut in; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: That leaves the other half of the belief: that using these tools well is a skill of its own, and the skilled pull ahead.

scenes.purpose: METR's tool-experience check: the one speedup vanished after a correction.

visual.description: Two stat tiles for the over-50-hours group: 'roughly 25%' faster before the correction, then 'roughly 0%' after; the second tile arrives on 'roughly 0 percent' and the first dims.

chart.title: Over 50 hours of Cursor: estimated speedup
chart.note: Experience hours partly self-reported; the group is very small.

scenes.direction: Tiles build on s21; first tile dims as the second lands.
scenes.narration: Among those deeply experienced developers, the slowdown broadly did not shrink with up to 50 hours of Cursor experience, counting the hours they reported from before the study. One developer past 50 hours did see a speedup, but when a second developer corrected the experience they had reported, that group's estimate fell from roughly 25 percent faster to roughly 0 percent.

scenes.purpose: In the Google trial, prior AI use made no significant difference, and why that may be.

visual.description: List: the finding, then the possible reasons as the narration names them.
onScreenText: Prior AI use: no significant difference
Too little statistical power
A low usability floor
Prompting skills not universal yet

scenes.direction: Reasons build one by one as each is named; each reason gets its own beat.
scenes.narration: In the trial that leaned toward seniors, run with full-time Googlers, how often people already used AI tools made no significant difference to their speed with AI; among the possible reasons its authors offer are too little statistical power, a low usability floor where the benefits come quickly, and one feature needing prompting skills that may not be universal yet.

scenes.purpose: The clearest sign tool skill matters, with its limit: Java proficiency mattered more.

visual.description: The cited paragraph; 'the more AI-skilled' highlights, then the closing sentence on the proficient Java developer.

excerpt.highlight: building on code developed by a proficient Java developer mattered even more

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'mattered even more'.
scenes.narration: The clearest sign that tool skill matters comes from a maintainability trial: the more practised the original developer was with AI, the better the code scored on a code-health measure once someone else built on it, though that developer's proficiency in Java mattered even more.

scenes.purpose: Answer the first question and name the thread: what the developer already knew.

visual.description: List builds one line per sentence: the verdict, then the thread.
onScreenText: Nothing shows AI multiplying experts far more
It helped more where the developer knew less

citations.label: Cui et al., Copilot field experiments

scenes.direction: Line one lands on 'nothing shows'; line two on 'how much the developer already knew'.
scenes.narration: So across these trials, nothing shows AI multiplying experts far more than novices: several leaned toward the less experienced, though the field experiments' gaps were noisy and not significant and another trial's result awaits further studies, and the one hint the other way was not significant either. What runs through them is how much the developer already knew: the tool helped more for short-tenure developers in one trial and on unfamiliar issues in another, and helped less for maintainers on tasks they knew well.

scenes.purpose: Pose the second question.

visual.description: Question types on; 'slower' in accent.
onScreenText: How can it leave an expert slower on work they know best?

scenes.direction: Type on; hold before the answer.
scenes.narration: But how can a tool that writes code for you leave an expert slower on work they know best?

scenes.purpose: The maintainers rejected most generations, and rejecting cost time.

visual.description: One big stat tile: '<44%' of generations accepted; on s28 the tile shifts up as the wasted-time point is spoken.

chart.title: Cursor generations accepted
chart.note: An upper bound, not an exact share.

scenes.direction: Tile punches in on 'fewer than 44 percent'.
scenes.narration: Back with those maintainers, the answer starts with how often they took what the tool offered: they accepted fewer than 44 percent of Cursor's generations. When they turned one down, they reprompted or gave up, and the researchers saw significant time wasted reviewing, testing or modifying code before rejecting it.

scenes.purpose: Even accepted code cost checking time.

visual.description: Two horizontal bars: 75% read every line, 56% often made major changes; each grows as spoken.

chart.title: What the developers reported

points.label: Read every line the AI wrote
Often made major changes to clean it up

chart.note: Developers' own reports; bars are separate shares, not parts of a whole.

scenes.direction: Bars grow one per figure.
scenes.narration: Even accepted code cost time: 75 percent said they read every line the AI wrote, and 56 percent said they often had to make major changes to clean it up.

scenes.purpose: Engineers describe the same trade in their own words.

visual.description: Two quote lines, one per sentence, quoted words only.
onScreenText: "I'm probably not going to bother using Claude."
"I'm just going to go and do it myself."

scenes.direction: Second quote replaces the first.
scenes.narration: Engineers deciding when to hand work to Claude described the same trade; for a task under 10 minutes, one said, "I'm probably not going to bother using Claude." Another described a cold start: their team's codebase holds knowledge Claude does not have by default, so rather than iterate on the perfect prompt, "I'm just going to go and do it myself."

scenes.purpose: The same limit at company scale: review speed was the bottleneck.

visual.description: One stat tile: '5,359 files' migrated; 'review' line fades under it as the bottleneck is named.
onScreenText: Bottleneck: how fast engineers could review

scenes.direction: Tile on '5,359 files'; line on 'bottleneck'.
scenes.narration: The same limit shows up at larger scale: in one company's AI-assisted migration of 5,359 files, the bottleneck was how fast engineers could review the changes, so the team deliberately capped how many changes it generated each week.

scenes.purpose: A literature review names the verification gap and the skill it calls for.

visual.description: List builds one line per sentence: the gap, then the skills.
onScreenText: A verification gap
Verification and review may matter as much as writing code

scenes.direction: Line one on 'verification gap'.
scenes.narration: A review of what has been written about vibe coding names its central risk a verification gap: code generated faster than developers and their processes can verify its correctness, security and provenance. Its authors suggest that skill in verification, constraint specification and review may matter as much as skill in writing code.

scenes.purpose: The catch: supervising needs the skills overuse may erode; and checking is part of the experts' price.

visual.description: Quote card with the two quoted words only.
onScreenText: "paradox of supervision"

scenes.direction: Camera pushes in on the phrase; hold 1 s.
scenes.narration: And the study of engineers using Claude names the catch, a "paradox of supervision": using Claude effectively requires supervising it, and supervising it requires the very coding skills that may atrophy from overuse. That checking is part of the price those maintainers paid.

scenes.purpose: Leave the viewer with two questions to ask before handing work over.

visual.description: List builds one line per sentence.
onScreenText: How much of it do you already know?
Keep enough of the skill to check what it hands back

scenes.direction: Lines build per sentence; hold 1 s at the end.
scenes.narration: So before you hand a task to an assistant, ask yourself how much of it you already know, and how long checking its answer will take. And if you find yourself deleting most of what it writes, point it at the parts that are new to you, and keep enough of the skill to check what it hands back.
